claims.text: Conventionally processed bulk HfNbTaTiZr has a single-phase microstructure.
Available measurements concern bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework will combine first-principles calculations with corrections for point defects, dislocations, and oxygen-induced local distortions.
Defect configurations are relatively frozen in the near-0–200 K regime.
From 300 to 1200 K, enhanced atomic vibrations and oxygen interactions increase electron scattering.
Oxygen-related point defects, dislocations, and local lattice distortions modify electronic scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurities and intrinsic lattice defects provide additional electron-scattering centers.
Additional scattering from oxygen and intrinsic defects reduces conductivity relative to predictions for an ideal defect-free crystal.
At low temperatures, static defects cause a modest reduction in conductivity.
At high temperatures, thermally activated defect behavior coupled with oxygen-related scattering causes a more pronounced departure from perfect-lattice predictions.
The defect-inclusive model will predict lower and more temperature-accurate conductivity values in both specified temperature regimes.
In the 300–1200 K regime, the model will reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least 10–20% relative to traditional analytical models.
In the 0–200 K regime, the model will capture the modest conductivity effect of frozen defect configurations.
Existing analytical predictions for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Existing defect-free analytical predictions typically overestimate HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity, especially at high temperature.
The proposed model is applicable to bulk nominal HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen near 1 wt.% and a conventionally processed microstructure, over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model may not apply to significantly different oxygen contents, extreme processing-induced defect populations, or compositions outside nominal HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect- and oxygen-scattering contributions are sensitive to microstructural state and defect distribution.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 10–20% relative to the defect-free baseline in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
